title: GitOps & ArgoCD
summary: GitOps is an operational model where Git is the single source of truth for infrastructure and application state. ArgoCD is the leading GitOps tool for Kubernetes — it continuously reconciles the cluster state with what's defined in Git. The sandbox runs a live ArgoCD instance you can explore.

sections.title: GitOps principles: Git as the single source of truth
sections.body:
## What GitOps Is and Why It Was Invented

GitOps is an operational model, not a specific tool. It is the practice of using Git as the authoritative source of truth for both application configuration and infrastructure state, and using automated agents to continuously reconcile the running system to match what Git says it should be.

**The problem GitOps solves:** In traditional deployments, the cluster's actual state and what you think is deployed gradually diverge. Someone applied a hotfix directly with `kubectl`. A failed deployment was partially rolled back. A secret was updated in place. Over time, no one is sure what is actually running, and rollback means manually reverse-engineering changes rather than running a single command. This is called **configuration drift**.

**The push model's security problem:** Traditional CI/CD gives the CI system direct write access to the production cluster. The CI runner holds a kubeconfig or cloud credentials. If the CI system is compromised — through a malicious dependency, a pipeline injection attack, or a misconfigured secret — the attacker has direct access to apply anything to production. This is a large attack surface that the GitOps pull model eliminates.

**The pull model's security advantage:** In GitOps, the CI system only writes to Git. The agent running *inside* the cluster (ArgoCD, Flux) pulls from Git and applies changes. External systems never need write access to the cluster. The blast radius of a CI compromise is limited to the Git repository, which has its own access controls and full audit history.

**Git as an audit log:** Every change to the system goes through a Git commit with an author, a timestamp, a commit message, and a diff. Rolling back to any previous state is `git revert`. Understanding what changed between two points in time is `git diff`. No separate change management database is needed — Git provides it for free.

**Repository structure is an architectural decision.** Whether to use a mono-repo or separate app and config repos, and whether environments are directories or branches, has real implications for developer experience, security boundaries, and operational complexity. The patterns shown in this section are all used in production; the right choice depends on team size and organizational structure.

GitOps applies the Git workflow to infrastructure operations. Instead of running kubectl commands or Terraform manually, you commit changes to Git and an automated agent applies them.

**The four GitOps principles (OpenGitOps):**

```
1. Declarative
   The desired system state is expressed declaratively.
   (Kubernetes YAML, Terraform HCL — not imperative kubectl commands)

2. Versioned and Immutable
   All desired state is stored in Git.
   History, audit trail, rollback via git revert.

3. Pulled Automatically
   Software agents pull the desired state and apply it.
   (Pull model, not push — CI pushes to Git, agent pulls from Git)

4. Continuously Reconciled
   Agents continuously observe actual state and reconcile
   to the desired state. Drift is detected and corrected.
```

**GitOps vs traditional CI/CD (push model):**

```
Traditional (Push):
  Developer → CI → kubectl apply → Cluster
  Problem: credentials in CI, no drift detection,
           manual rollback, no audit trail of who applied what

GitOps (Pull):
  Developer → Git commit → [GitOps agent watches repo] → Cluster
  Agent (ArgoCD/Flux) pulls from Git and applies changes.
  Benefits:
    - No kubectl credentials in CI
    - Automatic drift correction
    - Git history = full audit trail
    - Rollback = git revert
    - PR review = change approval
```

**Repository structure patterns:**

```
Pattern 1: Mono-repo
gitops-repo/
├── apps/
│   ├── web-app/
│   │   ├── deployment.yaml
│   │   └── service.yaml
│   └── api/
│       ├── deployment.yaml
│       └── service.yaml
└── infrastructure/
    ├── monitoring/
    └── cert-manager/

Pattern 2: Separate app and config repos
  app-repo/    ← source code + Dockerfile (developers own this)
  gitops-repo/ ← Kubernetes manifests (ops owns this)
               CI updates image tags here after building

Pattern 3: Environments as branches/directories
gitops-repo/
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   ├── staging/
│   └── production/
└── base/    ← shared base manifests (Kustomize)
```

sections.title: ArgoCD architecture and core concepts
sections.body:
## How ArgoCD Implements the GitOps Model

ArgoCD is a Kubernetes-native application that implements GitOps by running as a set of controllers inside your cluster. Understanding its architecture helps you reason about what it can and cannot do, how it fails, and how to troubleshoot it.

**ArgoCD installs into Kubernetes and manages Kubernetes.** This is unusual but deliberate: by running inside the cluster, ArgoCD uses the cluster's own RBAC system for authorization, uses cluster-native service accounts rather than external credentials, and is highly available through standard Kubernetes mechanisms. It manages itself and everything else through the same Kubernetes API.

**Three core components:**
- The **API Server** exposes the ArgoCD REST/gRPC API and serves the web UI. It is the entry point for all human interaction — `argocd` CLI commands and browser-based operations both hit this component.
- The **Repo Server** clones Git repositories and renders manifests. It handles Helm template rendering, Kustomize builds, and plain YAML. It is the component that needs network access to your Git repositories.
- The **Application Controller** is the reconciliation loop. It continuously compares the desired state (from the Repo Server's rendered manifests) against the actual state (from the Kubernetes API) and drives the cluster toward the desired state.

**Sync status and health status are independent dimensions.** A common source of confusion is treating them as a single status. An application can be `Synced` (cluster matches Git) but `Degraded` (the pods are crashing). It can be `Healthy` but `OutOfSync` (someone ran `kubectl edit` and changed something that Git does not reflect). Monitoring both dimensions is essential for a complete picture.

**`selfHeal: true`** is the operational embodiment of GitOps. When enabled, ArgoCD watches for any change to the cluster resources it manages and immediately reverts them to match Git. This is not just a convenience feature — it is a security control. Manual changes to production Kubernetes resources become impossible to persist when ArgoCD is self-healing. Every change must go through Git.

**`prune: true`** means resources that exist in the cluster but are not present in Git will be deleted. Without pruning, removing a resource from Git leaves it running in the cluster indefinitely — the cluster drifts from Git. With pruning enabled, deleting a resource from Git is sufficient to remove it from the cluster.

ArgoCD is a Kubernetes controller that watches Git repositories and synchronizes cluster state to match.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         ArgoCD                                  │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  │
│  │  API Server       │  │  Repo Server      │  │  Application │  │
│  │  (UI + CLI)       │  │  (git clone,      │  │  Controller  │  │
│  │                   │  │   render charts)  │  │  (reconcile) │  │
│  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────┘  │
│                                                                 │
└───────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┘
            │ reads                               │ applies
            ▼                                     ▼
      Git Repository                       Kubernetes Cluster
      (desired state)                      (actual state)
```

**Key ArgoCD objects:**

```
Application     — the core unit: watches a Git path, syncs to a namespace
                  "sync this directory in Git to this namespace in K8s"

AppProject      — groups Applications with access control
                  defines allowed source repos, destination clusters

ApplicationSet  — generates Applications dynamically
                  (one template → multiple apps: one per environment)

SyncPolicy      — manual vs automated sync
                  automated: ArgoCD syncs when Git changes
                  selfHeal: corrects manual kubectl changes
                  prune: deletes K8s resources removed from Git
```

**Sync status vs health status:**

```
Sync Status:
  Synced      — cluster matches Git
  OutOfSync   — cluster differs from Git
  Unknown     — cannot determine

Health Status:
  Healthy     — all resources are healthy
  Progressing — rolling update in progress
  Degraded    — something is wrong
  Missing     — resource doesn't exist in cluster

These are independent:
  Synced + Healthy    → everything good
  Synced + Degraded   → Git applied but app broken
  OutOfSync + Healthy → manual change made to cluster
```

**ArgoCD CLI:**

```bash
# The sandbox has ArgoCD running
# Port-forward to access the UI:
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:80 &
# Then visit: http://localhost:8080
# Default password:
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d && echo

# Install argocd CLI
# (already installed in sandbox — install elsewhere with:)
# curl -sSL -o argocd https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/releases/latest/download/argocd-linux-amd64
# chmod +x argocd && mv argocd /usr/local/bin/

# Login
argocd login localhost:8080 --username admin --password $(kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d) --insecure

# List apps
argocd app list

# Get app details
argocd app get <app-name>

# Sync an app manually
argocd app sync <app-name>

# Rollback to a previous version
argocd app rollback <app-name> <revision>

# Diff: what would change if synced now?
argocd app diff <app-name>
```

sections.title: Defining ArgoCD Applications
sections.body:
## The ArgoCD Application: Connecting Git to Kubernetes

The `Application` custom resource is the fundamental unit of ArgoCD. Every application you want ArgoCD to manage requires one. Understanding its structure — source, destination, and sync policy — is the core skill of GitOps operations.

**The source-destination model:** An ArgoCD Application always defines two things: *where to get the desired state from* (the source — a Git repo, a specific path, a specific revision) and *where to apply it* (the destination — a Kubernetes cluster and namespace). ArgoCD continuously reconciles these two. The source is always Git; the destination is always a Kubernetes API endpoint.

**`targetRevision`** controls which Git state ArgoCD tracks. `HEAD` means the latest commit on the default branch — suitable for automated continuous deployment. A specific branch name like `main` is also `HEAD` of that branch. A tag like `v1.2.3` or a specific commit SHA makes the application track a fixed, immutable point in history — useful for production environments where you want explicit control over when changes are applied.

**`syncPolicy.automated`** is what makes ArgoCD a continuous deployment system rather than just a deployment tool. Without `automated`, ArgoCD detects changes in Git but requires a human or CI system to trigger the sync. With `automated`, any push to the tracked Git path triggers an automatic sync within a few minutes. `prune` and `selfHeal` within the automated block control the two-way enforcement: Git → cluster (sync) and cluster → Git (selfHeal).

**The App of Apps pattern** is ArgoCD's solution to the bootstrapping problem: if ArgoCD manages applications via `Application` resources, who creates those `Application` resources? The answer is ArgoCD itself. A single root `Application` points to a directory containing other `Application` manifests. Syncing the root app creates all the child apps. From that point, adding a new application to the cluster is as simple as committing a new `Application` YAML to the root directory and pushing.

**`ApplicationSet`** takes this further: instead of manually creating one `Application` per environment, an `ApplicationSet` generates them from a template. The `list` generator shown here creates one application per environment element. More powerful generators include `git` (one app per directory in a repo) and `clusters` (one app per registered cluster). This is how platform teams manage dozens of applications across dozens of clusters without manual repetition.

**Sync waves** (`argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation) control ordering within a single sync operation. Resources with a lower wave number sync first. This is how you ensure that a database migration job completes before the application deployment that depends on it, or that namespaces and CRDs exist before the resources that use them.

An ArgoCD Application manifest tells ArgoCD what Git path to watch and where to deploy it.

**Basic Application (plain YAML from Git):**

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: argocd
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2"  # order within a sync
spec:
  project: default

  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/gitops-repo
    targetRevision: HEAD           # branch, tag, or commit SHA
    path: apps/web-app             # directory in the repo

  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc  # in-cluster
    namespace: production

  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true         # delete K8s resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true      # revert manual kubectl changes
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true  # create namespace if not exists
      - PrunePropagationPolicy=foreground
    retry:
      limit: 3
      backoff:
        duration: 5s
        factor: 2
```

**Application with Helm chart:**

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: prometheus
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
    chart: kube-prometheus-stack
    targetRevision: 55.5.0         # pin chart version
    helm:
      releaseName: monitoring
      values: |
        grafana:
          enabled: true
          adminPassword: supersecret
        prometheus:
          prometheusSpec:
            retention: 15d
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: monitoring
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
```

**App of Apps pattern (bootstrap an entire cluster):**

```yaml
# The root app manages all other apps
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/gitops-repo
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: apps/root              # directory containing other Application manifests
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
```

```
gitops-repo/
└── apps/
    └── root/             ← root app watches this directory
        ├── web-app.yaml  ← Application manifest for web-app
        ├── api.yaml      ← Application manifest for api
        └── monitoring.yaml
```

**ApplicationSet (generate apps from a template):**

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: environments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - env: dev
            namespace: dev
          - env: staging
            namespace: staging
          - env: production
            namespace: production
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'web-app-{{env}}'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/gitops-repo
        targetRevision: HEAD
        path: 'environments/{{env}}/web-app'
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: '{{namespace}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
```

sections.title: Exercise: explore ArgoCD in the sandbox
sections.body:
## Hands-On: Observing GitOps Reconciliation in Practice

Reading about GitOps principles is one thing; watching a live ArgoCD instance detect and correct drift is another. This exercise gives you direct experience with ArgoCD's core behavior: what happens when you break the GitOps contract by making a manual change to the cluster.

**What you are about to observe:** The exercise walks you through creating an ArgoCD Application pointed at a public example repository. Once ArgoCD syncs it, you will deliberately scale the deployment to a different replica count — a manual change that bypasses Git. With `selfHeal: true` enabled, ArgoCD will detect this drift and automatically revert the deployment to what Git specifies. The reversion typically happens within 3 minutes. This is the core GitOps guarantee made visible.

**The `OutOfSync` window:** Between the moment you make the manual change and the moment ArgoCD reverts it, the application will be in an `OutOfSync` state. Watch the sync status with `kubectl get application demo-app -n argocd -w`. You will see the status move from `Synced` to `OutOfSync` and back to `Synced` without any human intervention. In production, this automatic correction is what prevents accidental manual changes from persisting and creating configuration drift.

**The AppProject:** Every Application belongs to an AppProject. The `default` project allows access to any source repository and any destination. In production, AppProjects enforce security boundaries — restricting which repositories an Application can source from, which clusters and namespaces it can deploy to, and which Kubernetes resource types it is allowed to create. Inspect the default project at the end of the exercise to understand what it permits.

**Troubleshooting tip:** If `kubectl get pods -n argocd` shows any pods in a non-Running state, ArgoCD may not be fully operational. The most common causes in sandbox environments are resource pressure on the node and the repo-server failing to clone due to network restrictions. Check pod events with `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n argocd` if something looks wrong.

The sandbox has ArgoCD installed and running. Explore it with kubectl and the CLI.

```bash
# ── 1. Inspect the ArgoCD installation ────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get pods -n argocd
# Should see: argocd-server, argocd-repo-server, argocd-application-controller,
#             argocd-redis, argocd-dex-server

kubectl get svc -n argocd
# argocd-server exposes the UI and API

# ── 2. Get the initial admin password ─────────────────────────────────────
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d && echo
# Save this password

# ── 3. Port-forward the ArgoCD UI ─────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:80 &
echo "ArgoCD UI: http://localhost:8080 (username: admin)"

# ── 4. Check ArgoCD CRDs ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get crds | grep argoproj
# applications.argoproj.io
# applicationsets.argoproj.io
# appprojects.argoproj.io

# ── 5. Check existing applications (sandbox has demo apps) ────────────────
kubectl get applications -n argocd
kubectl get applications -n argocd -o yaml | head -60

# ── 6. Create a simple Application pointing to a public Git repo ──────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: demo-app
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/argoproj/argocd-example-apps
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: guestbook
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: guestbook
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
EOF

# ── 7. Watch it sync ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get application demo-app -n argocd -w
# Watch health and sync status change

# Check what it deployed:
kubectl get pods -n guestbook
kubectl get svc -n guestbook

# ── 8. Force an OutOfSync state ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Manually change something in the cluster:
kubectl scale deployment guestbook-ui -n guestbook --replicas=3

# ArgoCD detects drift and corrects it (selfHeal):
kubectl get application demo-app -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}'
# OutOfSync → then back to Synced after selfHeal kicks in
kubectl get deployment guestbook-ui -n guestbook
# Replicas should return to 1 (as defined in Git)

# ── 9. Inspect the AppProject ─────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get appproject default -n argocd -o yaml

# ── 10. Clean up
kubectl delete application demo-app -n argocd
kubectl delete namespace guestbook --ignore-not-found
```
